implementation_notes: ActiveRecord supplies the classic structure as a convention: if the table has an integer lock_version column, every update increments it and the write compares the value the record was loaded with, so a record instantiated twice lets the second save raise ActiveRecord::StaleObjectError (destroys are checked too); locking_column renames the column and lock_optimistically = false disables the behaviour. Sequel offers the same contract as an explicit plugin - plugin :optimistic_locking plus a lock_version column (default 0) makes the second update raise Sequel::NoExistingObject. Both replace the hand-written predicate and affected-row test; the application still owns the conflict policy (rescue, reload, merge or roll back), and the token is only as good as the write paths that go through the model.
code_sketch:
class Person < ApplicationRecord      # lock_version integer column
end

p1 = Person.find(1)
p2 = Person.find(1)
p1.update!(name: "Michael")
p2.update!(name: "Bob")             # => ActiveRecord::StaleObjectError
# Sequel: class Person < Sequel::Model; plugin :optimistic_locking; end
pitfalls: Only model saves are checked: update_all, delete_all, raw SQL, upsert and find_each(update) write without the token.
lock_version must default to 0 and be NOT NULL; a missing or NULL column disables the check silently.
The mechanism is per-process out of the box - across web workers lock_version must round-trip through the form (Rails documents adding it as a hidden field), or every request looks current.
Rescuing StaleObjectError and calling save! again without reload re-writes the stale attributes.

variants.name: Sequel optimistic_locking plugin
variants.implementation_notes: Sequel packages the same convention as an explicit plugin rather than a magic column name: load plugin :optimistic_locking on the model and the update/destroy instance filters gain the lock column, so a stale object raises Sequel::NoExistingObject; lock_column renames the column and the plugin builds on the instance_filters plugin, which means the check rides the normal filtered update. It is the choice for Sequel-based applications and for code bases that prefer an explicit declaration over ActiveRecord's implicit column convention.
variants.code_sketch:
class Person < Sequel::Model
  plugin :optimistic_locking
end
p1 = Person[1]
p2 = Person[1]
p1.update(name: "Jim")     # works
p2.update(name: "Bob")     # raises Sequel::NoExistingObject
pitfalls: The plugin depends on instance filters, so dataset-level updates (dataset.update, multi_insert) bypass the lock.
The lock column must exist and default to 0; a missing column makes updates raise instead of behaving optimistically.
